newsitem.title: PERU: Peru pledges to free more innocent prisoners.
newsitem.headline: Peru pledges to free more innocent prisoners.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori promised on Friday to continue a judicial review intended to free hundreds of prisoners thought to be wrongly accused of terrorism.

"I believe we must continue the liberation of the people unjustly imprisoned," Fujimori said in a speech, adding that he would seek an extension of the August deadline for the special state commission recommending pardons.
Earlier this week, Fujimori released 114 prisoners unjustly accused of terrorism during the state's ongoing war against leftist guerrillas.

That raised to more than 200 the number released since the commission was established in 1996. The government says another 200 will likely be freed in coming months, but rights groups say up to 800 more innocent people remain behind bars.
"We have to recognise that in the last few years inevitable excesses were committed that must be corrected," Fujimori said.

Peru's "faceless" courts, which Fujimori established in 1992 at the height of the state's war on the Shining Path and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrilla movements, have imprisoned about 4,000 people on terrorist charges.

The judges in these courts wear hoods over their heads or sit behind screens to protect their identities. Pardoned prisoners have said they were convicted on flimsy evidence, often obtained under torture or on the word of one informant, and without a proper defence.

The pardons commission was suspended since the Dec. 17 storming of the Japanese ambassador's residence by MRTA guerrillas who held 72 hostages for 126 days to demand the release of hundreds of their jailed comrades.

But Justice Minister Carlos Hermoza Moya said Fujimori restarted the review process this week due to his "willingness to resolve the situation of these people who were condemned on the basis of evidence taken to an exaggerated degree by the tribunals."
The MRTA hostage-takers were killed, without obtaining any releases, in an April 22 military rescue that also left one hostage and two soldiers dead.
